title: Mumbai's Iconic Ashok Vada Pav Earns Global Recognition on TasteAtlas' World's Most Iconic Sandwiches List
excerpt: The 60-year-old Dadar street stall that invented vada pav has been ranked 25th among the world's most iconic sandwiches by the global food guide, putting Mumbai's signature snack on the international map.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ashok Vada Pav ranks 25th on TasteAtlas' World's Most Iconic Sandwiches list.
  • The stall has been serving vada pav since 1978, invented by Ashok Vaidya in the 1960s.
  • A single vada pav costs ₹35, making it one of the cheapest iconic sandwiches globally.
  • Top three sandwiches on the list include Turkey's Tombik Döner, Vietnam's Bánh Mì Heo Quay, and Lebanon's Shawarma.

  • Mumbai's Ashok Vada Pav has been ranked 25th on TasteAtlas' list of the World's Most Iconic Sandwiches, and is recommended as the top place to try vada pav globally.
  • The stall near Kirti College in Dadar has operated since 1978 and traces its roots to Ashok Vaidya, widely credited with inventing vada pav in the 1960s.
  • A single vada pav at the stall costs ₹35, making it one of the cheapest entries on a list that spans 100 sandwiches from around the world.
  • Turkey's Tombik Döner, Vietnam's Bánh Mì Heo Quay, and Venezuela's Arepa Reina Pepiada topped the list.

For anyone who has navigated the crush of Dadar station during rush hour, the sight is familiar: a queue snaking around a modest stall near Kirti College, where the smell of deep-fried potato vadas cuts through the diesel and sea air. Ashok Vada Pav has been feeding Mumbai's commuters, students, and construction workers since 1978. Now, global food guide TasteAtlas has placed it among the 100 most iconic sandwiches on earth.

The listing ranks vada pav 25th overall and singles out Ashok Vada Pav as the number one place in the world to try the dish. It sits alongside Turkey's Tombik Döner (first), Vietnam's Bánh Mì Heo Quay (second), and Lebanon's Shawarma (fifth) — each a street food with deep working-class roots that has traveled far from its origins.

An Epiphany Outside Dadar Station

The invention of vada pav belongs to Ashok Vaidya, a street vendor who worked the pavements outside Dadar station in the late 1960s. The batata vada — a spiced, deep-fried potato ball — was already a fixture of Maharashtrian snacking, but it had a problem: hot vadas didn't travel well, and cold ones weren't worth eating.

"Carbs inside carbs, illogical and irresistible."

Vaidya's solution, in what food historian Kurush Dalal has described as "an absolute epiphany," was to stuff the vada into a pav — the soft white bread roll that Goan migrants and later Muslim and Irani bakers had brought to Bombay. Carbs inside carbs, illogical and irresistible. A meal that cost almost nothing, could be eaten with one hand, and fueled a city that ran on textile mills and train schedules.

The stall that Ashok Thakur set up in 1978 near Kirti College carried that tradition forward. His wife Aparna and brother Manohar still run it. A single vada pav costs ₹35 — roughly 42 cents — making it among the cheapest items on the entire TasteAtlas list.

Mumbai's Edible Identity

Vada pav is not simply popular in Mumbai. It is structural. It feeds an estimated two to three million people daily across the city — from construction laborers at dawn to college students between lectures to Bollywood actors photographed eating them at film shoots. It has survived the arrival of international fast-food chains, the explosion of food delivery apps, and periodic regulatory crackdowns on street vending.

The dish's construction is deceptively precise. The vada must be fried at the right temperature — too hot and the exterior burns before the potato cooks through; too low and the coating absorbs oil. The pav is ideally fresh and slightly warm. The chutney — a fiery red paste of coconut, peanuts, garlic, tamarind, and chilies — is where each stall establishes its identity.

At Ashok Vada Pav, the signature addition is chivda, the fried batter bits that add texture and crunch. Regulars know to ask for it. Tourists, increasingly, are learning.

From Street Corner to Global Lists

This is not vada pav's first brush with international food rankings — TasteAtlas ranked it 19th in an earlier "best sandwiches" list, and 28th in a subsequent one. The rankings fluctuate, but the direction is consistently upward. Each listing generates a fresh wave of social media engagement and, inevitably, the same indignant question from Mumbaikars: why isn't it higher?

For the Indian diaspora, the recognition carries a particular warmth. Vada pav is the food of arrivals and departures — eaten at railway stations, bus stops, and airport approaches. For Indians abroad, it is the taste most difficult to replicate authentically and the one most immediately missed. No international Indian restaurant chain has cracked it, partly because its magic is inseparable from its context: the stall, the queue, the paper-wrapped parcel eaten standing up.

The TasteAtlas listing won't change that. But it does something quieter: it tells the world that a ₹35 snack from a 60-year-old stall in Dadar belongs in the same conversation as the döner, the bánh mì, and the lobster roll. For a dish born to feed workers who couldn't afford to sit down, that's a kind of vindication its inventor might have appreciated.
